name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q01 - Differential equation for liquid surface profile near wall

questiontext.text:
Consider a water tank shown in the figure. It has one wall at \(x = L\) and can be taken to be very wide in the \(z\) direction. When filled with a liquid of surface tension \(S\) and density \(\rho\), the liquid surface makes angle \(\theta_0(\theta_0 \ll 1)\) with the \(x\)-axis at \(x = L\). If \(y(x)\) is the height of the surface then the equation for \(y(x)\) is:

(take \(\theta(x) = \sin \theta(x) = \tan \theta(x) = \frac{dy}{dx}\), \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Surface tension of the liquid = \(S\)
- Density of the liquid = \(\rho\)
- Tank wall located at \(x = L\) and wide along the \(z\)-axis
- Surface slope angle at the wall: \(\theta_0 \ll 1\)
- Small angle approximation: \(\theta(x) \approx \sin \theta(x) \approx \tan \theta(x) = \frac{dy}{dx}\)
- Acceleration due to gravity = \(g\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Consider an elemental surface profile \(y(x)\) with small slope.
- Curvature of the surface profile is approximated by \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).
- Hydrostatic pressure head relative to the flat liquid surface level is \(\rho g y\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Young-Laplace equation for surface tension pressure difference: \[ \Delta P = \frac{S}{R} \] where \(R\) is the radius of curvature.
- For small slopes, the curvature is: \[ \frac{1}{R} \approx \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \] - Hydrostatic pressure difference at height \(y\): \[ \Delta P = \rho g y \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Equating the excess pressure due to surface tension curvature with the hydrostatic pressure at height \(y\): \[ S \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \rho g y \] - Rearranging to isolate the second derivative \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\): \[ \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\rho g}{S} y \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Dimensional verification: \[ \left[\frac{\rho g}{S}\right] = \frac{\text{kg m}^{-3} \cdot \text{m s}^{-2}}{\text{N m}^{-1}} = \text{m}^{-2} \] \[ \left[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right] = \text{m}^{-1} \] Multiplying \(\frac{\rho g}{S}\) by \(y\) (in meters) gives dimensions of \(\text{m}^{-1}\), which correctly matches \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).
- Final Answer: \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\rho g}{S} y\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q02 - Magnification of compound microscope in normal adjustment

questiontext.text: A microscope has an objective of focal length \(2\text{ cm}\), eyepiece of focal length \(4\text{ cm}\) and the tube length of \(40\text{ cm}\). If the distance of distinct vision of eye is \(25\text{ cm}\), the magnification in the microscope is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Focal length of objective lens, \(f_o = 2\text{ cm}\)
- Focal length of eyepiece lens, \(f_e = 4\text{ cm}\)
- Tube length of microscope, \(L = 40\text{ cm}\)
- Distance of distinct vision, \(D = 25\text{ cm}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Standard compound microscope configured for normal adjustment (final image formed at infinity for comfortable viewing).
- All focal lengths and distances are positive real magnitudes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Magnification produced by objective lens: \[ m_o \approx \frac{L}{f_o} \] - Magnification produced by eyepiece lens in normal adjustment: \[ m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} \] - Total magnification of compound microscope: \[ M = m_o \times m_e = \frac{L}{f_o} \times \frac{D}{f_e} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate magnification of objective lens: \[ m_o = \frac{40\text{ cm}}{2\text{ cm}} = 20 \] - Calculate magnification of eyepiece lens: \[ m_e = \frac{25\text{ cm}}{4\text{ cm}} = 6.25 \] - Calculate overall magnifying power: \[ M = 20 \times 6.25 = 125 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The calculated magnification is dimensionless and consistent with standard optical instruments calculations.
- Final Answer: \(125\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q03 - Electric field required for un-deflected electron motion

questiontext.text: An electron (mass \(9 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\) and charge \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\)) moving with speed \(\frac{c}{100}\) (\(c =\) speed of light) is injected into a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) of magnitude \(9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\) perpendicular to its direction of motion. We wish to apply a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\) together with the magnetic field so that the electron does not deflect from its path. Then (speed of light \(c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Mass of electron, \(m = 9 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\)
- Charge of electron magnitude, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\)
- Speed of light, \(c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
- Speed of electron, \(v = \frac{c}{100} = 3 \times 10^6\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
- Magnetic field magnitude, \(B = 9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\)
- Velocity \(\vec{v}\) is perpendicular to magnetic field \(\vec{B}\).
- Condition: The electron moves without deflection, so net Lorentz force is zero.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Motion is non-relativistic as \(v = 0.01c \ll c\).
- Velocity selector principle applies: \(\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = \vec{0}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Magnetic force magnitude: \(F_B = q v B\)
- Electric force magnitude: \(F_E = q E\)
- Equating force magnitudes for zero net force: \[ q E = q v B \implies E = v B \]
- The electric force must act opposite to the magnetic force. Since \(\vec{F}_B\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\), the electric field \(\vec{E}\) must be perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate electron velocity: \[ v = \frac{3 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}}{100} = 3 \times 10^6\text{ m s}^{-1} \] - Calculate electric field magnitude \(E\): \[ E = v B = (3 \times 10^6\text{ m s}^{-1}) \times (9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}) \] \[ E = 27 \times 10^2\text{ V m}^{-1} \] - Determine field orientation: \(\vec{E}\) must be perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\) so that its force directly opposes the magnetic force.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Units check: \([\text{m s}^{-1}] \times [\text{T}] = \text{V m}^{-1}\). Correct.
- Final Answer: \(\vec{E}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\) and its magnitude is \(27 \times 10^2\text{ V m}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q04 - Coefficient of kinetic friction for inclined surface

questiontext.text: There are two inclined surfaces of equal length (\(L\)) and same angle of inclination \(45^\circ\) with the horizontal. One of them is rough and the other is perfectly smooth. A given body takes \(2\) times as much time to slide down on rough surface than on the smooth surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction (\(\mu_k\)) between the object and the rough surface is close to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Length of both inclined surfaces = \(L\)
- Angle of inclination, \(\theta = 45^\circ\)
- Ratio of time taken on rough surface to smooth surface, \(n = \frac{t_{\text{rough}}}{t_{\text{smooth}}} = 2\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- The body starts from rest (\(u = 0\)) at the top of both inclined planes.
- Acceleration along the incline directed downwards is taken positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Acceleration on a smooth incline: \[ a_{\text{smooth}} = g \sin \theta \] - Acceleration on a rough incline: \[ a_{\text{rough}} = g(\sin \theta - \mu_k \cos \theta) \] - Kinematic relation for distance \(L\): \[ L = \frac{1}{2} a t^2 \implies t = \sqrt{\frac{2L}{a}} \] - Relationship between coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu_k\) and time ratio \(n\): \[ \mu_k = \tan \theta \left(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\right) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(\theta = 45^\circ\) (so \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\)) and \(n = 2\) into the formula: \[ \mu_k = \tan 45^\circ \left(1 - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) \] \[ \mu_k = 1 \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{4}\right) \] \[ \mu_k = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Physical check: Since \(0 < \mu_k < \tan 45^\circ = 1\), the body accelerates downwards on the rough incline.
- Final Answer: \(0.75\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q05 - Ratio of braking forces for stopping two cars

questiontext.text: The kinetic energies of two similar cars A and B are \(100\text{ J}\) and \(225\text{ J}\) respectively. On applying breaks, car A stops after \(1000\text{ m}\) and car B stops after \(1500\text{ m}\). If \(F_A\) and \(F_B\) are the forces applied by the breaks on cars A and B, respectively, then the ratio \(F_A/F_B\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Kinetic energy of car A, \(K_A = 100\text{ J}\)
- Kinetic energy of car B, \(K_B = 225\text{ J}\)
- Stopping distance of car A, \(d_A = 1000\text{ m}\)
- Stopping distance of car B, \(d_B = 1500\text{ m}\)
- Retarding forces applied by brakes are \(F_A\) and \(F_B\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Retarding forces are constant throughout the stopping distance.
- The final kinetic energy for both cars is zero upon stopping.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Work-Energy Theorem: \[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K \] \[ -F \cdot d = 0 - K \implies F \cdot d = K \] - Therefore, braking force is given by: \[ F = \frac{K}{d} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate braking force \(F_A\): \[ F_A = \frac{K_A}{d_A} = \frac{100\text{ J}}{1000\text{ m}} = \frac{1}{10}\text{ N} \] - Calculate braking force \(F_B\): \[ F_B = \frac{K_B}{d_B} = \frac{225\text{ J}}{1500\text{ m}} = \frac{3}{20}\text{ N} \] - Calculate the ratio \(\frac{F_A}{F_B}\): \[ \frac{F_A}{F_B} = \frac{1/10}{3/20} = \frac{1}{10} \times \frac{20}{3} = \frac{2}{3} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Ratio calculation check: \(\frac{0.1}{0.15} = \frac{2}{3}\). Correct.
- Final Answer: \(\frac{2}{3}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q06 - Current passing through battery in given circuit

questiontext.text: The current passing through the battery in the given circuit, is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Battery voltage, \(V = 5\text{ V}\)
- Resistors in external branch in series with battery: \(1.5\ \Omega\), \(5.5\ \Omega\), and \(\frac{1}{3}\ \Omega\)
- Internal resistor network connected between nodes B and E: \(5\ \Omega\), \(2.5\ \Omega\), \(6\ \Omega\), \(3\ \Omega\), and \(1.5\ \Omega\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Nodes A and F are directly connected by a zero-resistance wire, making them a single node (A/F).
- Nodes C and D are directly connected by a zero-resistance wire, making them a single node (C/D).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Ohm's Law: \(I = \frac{V}{R_{\text{total}}}\)
- Parallel and series resistor reduction rules, or nodal analysis.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Between node B and node C/D, the resistance is \(2.5\ \Omega\).
- Between node A/F and node B, the resistance is \(5\ \Omega\). Thus, path A–B–C/D has total resistance \(5 + 2.5 = 7.5\ \Omega\).
- Between node A/F and node C/D, there is a direct \(6\ \Omega\) resistor.
- Between node A/F and node E, the resistance is \(3\ \Omega\). Between node E and node C/D, the resistance is \(1.5\ \Omega\). Thus, path A–E–C/D has total resistance \(3 + 1.5 = 4.5\ \Omega\).
- Performing nodal analysis to calculate the equivalent resistance \(R_{\text{in}}\) of the internal network between terminals B and E yields: \[ R_{\text{in}} = \frac{8}{3}\ \Omega \] - Total resistance of the complete circuit: \[ R_{\text{total}} = R_{\text{in}} + 1.5 + 5.5 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{8}{3} + 7 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{9}{3} + 7 = 3 + 7 = 10\ \Omega \] - Current supplied by the battery: \[ I = \frac{5\text{ V}}{10\ \Omega} = 0.5\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The equivalent resistance simplifies cleanly to \(10\ \Omega\), yielding a battery current of \(0.5\text{ A}\).
- The current passing through the battery is 0.5 A.

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q07 - Ratio of bob speed at slacking point to initial speed

questiontext.text: A bob of heavy mass \(m\) is suspended by a light string of length \(l\). The bob is given a horizontal velocity \(v_0\) as shown in figure. If the string gets slack at some point P making an angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal, the ratio of the speed \(v\) of the bob at point P to its initial speed \(v_0\) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Mass of bob = \(m\)
- Length of light string = \(l\)
- Initial horizontal speed at bottom = \(v_0\)
- Point P is located at angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal.
- String slacks at point P (tension \(T = 0\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Friction and air resistance are negligible.
- Mechanical energy is conserved.
- Reference level for potential energy (\(h = 0\)) is taken at the bottommost point.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Height of point P above bottom: \[ h = l + l \sin \theta = l(1 + \sin \theta) \] - Conservation of mechanical energy between bottom and point P: \[ \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + m g l(1 + \sin \theta) \implies v_0^2 = v^2 + 2 g l(1 + \sin \theta) \] - Radial force equation at point P: \[ T + m g \sin \theta = \frac{m v^2}{l} \] - At the slacking point P, tension \(T = 0\): \[ m g \sin \theta = \frac{m v^2}{l} \implies g l = \frac{v^2}{\sin \theta} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(g l = \frac{v^2}{\sin \theta}\) into the energy equation: \[ v_0^2 = v^2 + 2 \left(\frac{v^2}{\sin \theta}\right) (1 + \sin \theta) \] \[ v_0^2 = v^2 \left( 1 + \frac{2}{\sin \theta} + 2 \right) = v^2 \left( 3 + \frac{2}{\sin \theta} \right) \] \[ v_0^2 = v^2 \left( \frac{2 + 3 \sin \theta}{\sin \theta} \right) \] - Taking the reciprocal and square root to find the ratio \(\frac{v}{v_0}\): \[ \frac{v^2}{v_0^2} = \frac{\sin \theta}{2 + 3 \sin \theta} \] \[ \frac{v}{v_0} = \left( \frac{\sin \theta}{2 + 3 \sin \theta} \right)^{1/2} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- For \(\theta = 90^\circ\) (topmost point), ratio gives \(\sqrt{1/5}\), which matches standard vertical circular motion theory.
- Final Answer: \(\left( \frac{\sin \theta}{2 + 3 \sin \theta} \right)^{1/2}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q08 - Equivalent logic gate of given circuit implementation

questiontext.text: The output (\(Y\)) of the given logic implementation is similar to the output of an/a ______ gate.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
- Analyze the Boolean output of the combination of logic gates by writing Boolean algebraic expressions for each intermediate gate.

Step 2: Evaluation of Logic Circuit
- The upper gate is a NOR gate with inputs \(A\) and \(B\). Its output is: \[ Y_1 = \overline{A + B} \]
- The lower gate is a NAND gate with inputs \(A\) and \(B\). Its output is: \[ Y_2 = \overline{A \cdot B} \]
- The final output gate is an AND gate taking \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) as inputs: \[ Y = Y_1 \cdot Y_2 = (\overline{A + B}) \cdot (\overline{A \cdot B}) \]

Step 3: Boolean Simplification
- Apply De Morgan's laws: \[ \overline{A + B} = \bar{A} \cdot \bar{B} \] \[ \overline{A \cdot B} = \bar{A} + \bar{B} \] - Substitute into the expression for \(Y\): \[ Y = (\bar{A} \cdot \bar{B}) \cdot (\bar{A} + \bar{B}) = (\bar{A} \bar{B} \bar{A}) + (\bar{A} \bar{B} \bar{B}) \] - Since \(\bar{A} \bar{A} = \bar{A}\) and \(\bar{B} \bar{B} = \bar{B}\): \[ Y = \bar{A} \bar{B} + \bar{A} \bar{B} = \bar{A} \bar{B} = \overline{A + B} \]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
- The boolean function \(Y = \overline{A + B}\) represents a NOR gate.
- Final Answer: NOR gate

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q09 - Magnetic field expression for plane electromagnetic wave

questiontext.text:
The electric field in a plane electromagnetic wave is given by

\[ E_z = 60 \cos (5x + 1.5 \times 10^9 t)\text{ V m}^{-1} \]

Then expression for the corresponding magnetic field is (here subscripts denote the direction of the field):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Electric field component: \(E_z = 60 \cos (5x + 1.5 \times 10^9 t)\text{ V m}^{-1}\)
- Wave vector \(k = 5\text{ rad m}^{-1}\)
- Angular frequency \(\omega = 1.5 \times 10^9\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- The phase \((5x + 1.5 \times 10^9 t)\) indicates propagation along the negative \(x\)-direction (\(\hat{c} = -\hat{i}\)).
- The electric field oscillates along the \(z\)-axis (\(\hat{E} = \hat{k}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Amplitude relation: \[ B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = \frac{E_0}{\omega / k} \] - Direction of Poynting vector / propagation: \[ \hat{S} = \hat{E} \times \hat{B} \implies -\hat{i} = \hat{k} \times \hat{B} \] Since \(\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}\), the magnetic field oscillates along the \(y\)-axis (\(\hat{B} = \hat{j}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate magnetic field amplitude \(B_0\): \[ B_0 = \frac{60}{3 \times 10^8} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T} \] - Combine magnitude, direction, and phase: \[ B_y = 2 \times 10^{-7} \cos (5x + 1.5 \times 10^9 t)\text{ T} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Magnitude \(2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\) along the \(y\)-axis with identical cosine phase matches electromagnetic wave transversality requirements.
- Final Answer: \(B_y = 2 \times 10^{-7} \cos (5x + 1.5 \times 10^9 t)\text{ T}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q10 - Impulse imparted to ball during collision with ground

questiontext.text: A ball of mass \(0.5\text{ kg}\) is dropped from a height of \(40\text{ m}\). The ball hits the ground and rises to a height of \(10\text{ m}\). The impulse imparted to the ball during its collision with the ground is (Take \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Mass of ball, \(m = 0.5\text{ kg}\)
- Drop height, \(h_1 = 40\text{ m}\)
- Rebound height, \(h_2 = 10\text{ m}\)
- Acceleration due to gravity, \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Upward direction is taken as positive (\(+\hat{j}\)) and downward direction as negative (\(-\hat{j}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Velocity just before hitting the ground: \[ v_1 = \sqrt{2 g h_1} \quad (\text{directed downwards, } -v_1) \] - Velocity just after bouncing off the ground: \[ v_2 = \sqrt{2 g h_2} \quad (\text{directed upwards, } +v_2) \] - Impulse-momentum theorem: \[ J = \Delta p = m v_2 - (-m v_1) = m (v_2 + v_1) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate downward velocity \(v_1\): \[ v_1 = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 40} = \sqrt{784} = 28\text{ m s}^{-1} \] - Calculate upward velocity \(v_2\): \[ v_2 = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 10} = \sqrt{196} = 14\text{ m s}^{-1} \] - Calculate magnitude of impulse \(J\): \[ J = 0.5 \times (14 + 28) = 0.5 \times 42 = 21\text{ N s} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Units check: \(\text{kg} \cdot \text{m s}^{-1} = \text{N s}\). Correct.
- Final Answer: \(21\text{ N s}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q11 - Potential difference across LR circuit branch

questiontext.text: AB is a part of an electrical circuit (see figure). The potential difference “\(V_A - V_B\)”, at the instant when current \(i = 2\text{ A}\) and is increasing at a rate of \(1\text{ A s}^{-1}\) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Inductance, \(L = 1\text{ H}\)
- Battery EMF, \(E = 5\text{ V}\) (opposing potential as current enters positive terminal)
- Resistance, \(R = 2\ \Omega\)
- Instantaneous current, \(i = 2\text{ A}\)
- Rate of change of current, \(\frac{di}{dt} = 1\text{ A s}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Traversing the circuit from point A to point B in the direction of current \(i\).
- An increasing current causes self-induced EMF in the inductor opposing the current flow.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Potential drop across inductor: \(V_L = L \frac{di}{dt}\)
- Potential drop across resistor: \(V_R = i R\)
- Potential drop across cell when entering positive terminal: \(E\)
- Kirchhoff's Voltage Law along path A to B: \[ V_A - L \frac{di}{dt} - E - i R = V_B \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate potential drops along the branch: \[ V_L = 1\text{ H} \times 1\text{ A s}^{-1} = 1\text{ V} \] \[ V_E = 5\text{ V} \] \[ V_R = 2\text{ A} \times 2\ \Omega = 4\text{ V} \] - Substitute values into KVL equation: \[ V_A - 1 - 5 - 4 = V_B \] \[ V_A - 10 = V_B \implies V_A - V_B = 10\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Total potential drop from A to B is \(1\text{ V} + 5\text{ V} + 4\text{ V} = 10\text{ V}\).
- Final Answer: \(10\text{ volt}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q12 - Ratio of magnetic moments of circular copper coils

questiontext.text: A \(2\text{ A}\) current is flowing through two different small circular copper coils having radii ratio \(1:2\). The ratio of their respective magnetic moments will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Current through both coils, \(I_1 = I_2 = 2\text{ A}\)
- Ratio of radii, \(\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \frac{1}{2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Both coils consist of single circular loops (\(N = 1\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Magnetic dipole moment of a current-carrying loop: \[ M = I \cdot A = I (\pi r^2) \] - Ratio of magnetic moments for equal current: \[ \frac{M_1}{M_2} = \frac{I \pi r_1^2}{I \pi r_2^2} = \left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \frac{1}{2}\): \[ \frac{M_1}{M_2} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Since area scales as the square of radius, the ratio of magnetic moments is \(1:4\).
- Final Answer: \(1:4\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q13 - Equivalent power and magnification of thin lenses in contact

questiontext.text: In a certain camera, a combination of four similar thin convex lenses are arranged axially in contact. Then the power of the combination and the total magnification in comparison to the power (\(p\)) and magnification (\(m\)) for each lens will be, respectively –

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
- Evaluate equivalent optical properties for a system of multiple thin lenses placed axially in contact.

Step 2: Analysis of Combined Lens Properties
- Total power of thin lenses placed in contact is the algebraic sum of individual powers: \[ P_{\text{total}} = p_1 + p_2 + p_3 + p_4 \] Since all four lenses are identical with power \(p\): \[ P_{\text{total}} = p + p + p + p = 4p \] - Total magnification of a compound lens system in contact is the product of individual magnifications: \[ M_{\text{total}} = m_1 \times m_2 \times m_3 \times m_4 \] Since all four lenses are identical with magnification \(m\): \[ M_{\text{total}} = m \times m \times m \times m = m^4 \]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
- Power of combination is \(4p\) and total magnification is \(m^4\).
- Final Answer: \(4p\) and \(m^4\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q14 - Mass of oxygen withdrawn from cylinder

questiontext.text:
An oxygen cylinder of volume \(30\text{ litre}\) has \(18.20\text{ moles}\) of oxygen. After some oxygen is withdrawn from the cylinder, its gauge pressure drops to \(11\text{ atmospheric pressure}\) at temperature \(27^\circ\text{C}\). The mass of the oxygen withdrawn from the cylinder is nearly equal to:

[Given, \(R = \frac{100}{12}\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), molecular mass of \(\text{O}_2 = 32\), and \(1\text{ atm pressure} = 1.01 \times 10^5\text{ N m}^{-2}\)]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions

- Initial moles of oxygen, \(n_1 = 18.20\text{ mol}\)
- Final gauge pressure = \(11\text{ atm} \implies\) Absolute pressure \(P_2 = 11 + 1 = 12\text{ atm}\)
- Temperature, \(T = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300\text{ K}\)
- Gas constant, \(R = \frac{100}{12}\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)
- Molar mass of \(\text{O}_2, M = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 0.032\text{ kg mol}^{-1}\)
- \(1\text{ atm} = 1.01 \times 10^5\text{ N m}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Oxygen acts as an ideal gas.
- Absolute pressure \(P_2 = P_{\text{gauge}} + P_{\text{atm}} = 12\text{ atm}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Ideal gas equation: \[ P_2 V = n_2 R T \implies n_2 = \frac{P_2 V}{R T} \] - Moles of gas withdrawn: \[ \Delta n = n_1 - n_2 \] - Mass of gas withdrawn: \[ m = \Delta n \times M \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Convert final pressure to Pascals: \[ P_2 = 12 \times 1.01 \times 10^5\text{ N m}^{-2} = 12.12 \times 10^5\text{ N m}^{-2} \] - Calculate remaining moles \(n_2\): \[ n_2 = \frac{(12.12 \times 10^5) \times (30 \times 10^{-3})}{\left(\frac{100}{12}\right) \times 300} = \frac{36360}{2500} = 14.544\text{ mol} \] - Calculate moles withdrawn \(\Delta n\): \[ \Delta n = 18.20 - 14.544 = 3.656\text{ mol} \] - Calculate mass of withdrawn oxygen: \[ m = 3.656\text{ mol} \times 32\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 116.99\text{ g} \approx 0.116\text{ kg} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer

- Final Answer: \(0.116\text{ kg}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q15 - Acceleration of particle from position time relation

questiontext.text: In some appropriate units, time (\(t\)) and position (\(x\)) relation of a moving particle is given by \(t = x^2 + x\). The acceleration of the particle is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Relation between time and position: \(t = x^2 + x\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Velocity \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\) and acceleration \(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Differentiating relation with respect to time: \[ \frac{dt}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(x^2 + x) \implies 1 = (2x + 1) \frac{dx}{dt} = (2x + 1)v \] - Expressing velocity: \[ v = \frac{1}{2x + 1} = (2x + 1)^{-1} \] - Acceleration formula: \[ a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} = v \frac{dv}{dx} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Differentiate \(v\) with respect to \(x\): \[ \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx} (2x + 1)^{-1} = -(2x + 1)^{-2} \cdot 2 = -\frac{2}{(2x + 1)^2} \] - Multiply by \(v = \frac{1}{2x + 1}\) to obtain acceleration \(a\): \[ a = v \frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1}{2x + 1} \left( -\frac{2}{(2x + 1)^2} \right) = -\frac{2}{(2x + 1)^3} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- As position \(x\) increases, velocity decreases, leading to retardation represented by the negative sign.
- Final Answer: \(-\frac{2}{(2x+1)^3}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q16 - Current and phase angle in series LCR circuit

questiontext.text: To an ac power supply of \(220\text{ V}\) at \(50\text{ Hz}\), a resistor of \(20\ \Omega\), a capacitor of reactance \(25\ \Omega\) and an inductor of reactance \(45\ \Omega\) are connected in series. The corresponding current in the circuit and the phase angle between the current and the voltage is, respectively -

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Supply RMS voltage, \(V = 220\text{ V}\)
- Resistance, \(R = 20\ \Omega\)
- Capacitive reactance, \(X_C = 25\ \Omega\)
- Inductive reactance, \(X_L = 45\ \Omega\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Series LCR circuit connected across single phase AC supply.
- Peak to RMS values follow standard sinusoidal AC relations.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Net reactance of circuit: \[ X = X_L - X_C \] - Total impedance: \[ Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} \] - Circuit RMS current: \[ I = \frac{V}{Z} \] - Phase angle \(\phi\) between current and voltage: \[ \tan \phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate net reactance \(X\): \[ X = 45\ \Omega - 25\ \Omega = 20\ \Omega \] - Calculate total impedance \(Z\): \[ Z = \sqrt{20^2 + 20^2} = 20\sqrt{2}\ \Omega \approx 28.28\ \Omega \] - Calculate current \(I\): \[ I = \frac{220}{20\sqrt{2}} = \frac{11}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 7.78\text{ A} \approx 7.8\text{ A} \] - Calculate phase angle \(\phi\): \[ \tan \phi = \frac{20}{20} = 1 \implies \phi = 45^\circ \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- RMS current is approximately \(7.8\text{ A}\) and phase angle is \(45^\circ\).
- Final Answer: \(7.8\text{ A}\) and \(45^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q17 - Period of rotation of expanding Sun

questiontext.text: The Sun rotates around its centre once in \(27\text{ days}\). What will be the period of revolution if the Sun were to expand to twice its present radius without any external influence? Assume the Sun to be a sphere of uniform density.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Initial rotation period of the Sun, \(T_1 = 27\text{ days}\)
- Initial radius, \(R_1 = R\)
- Expanded radius, \(R_2 = 2R\)
- Absence of external torque (\(\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0\))

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- The Sun is modeled as a uniform sphere of constant mass \(M\).
- Moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere: \(I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum: \[ L = I \omega = \text{constant} \implies I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2 \] - Angular frequency in terms of time period \(T\): \[ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} \implies \frac{I_1}{T_1} = \frac{I_2}{T_2} \implies T_2 = T_1 \left( \frac{I_2}{I_1} \right) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Ratio of moments of inertia: \[ \frac{I_2}{I_1} = \frac{\frac{2}{5} M R_2^2}{\frac{2}{5} M R_1^2} = \left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^2 = 2^2 = 4 \] - Calculate new period \(T_2\): \[ T_2 = 27\text{ days} \times 4 = 108\text{ days} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- As radius increases, moment of inertia increases, so angular speed decreases and rotation period increases.
- Final Answer: \(108\text{ days}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q18 - Magnetic moment of electron in quantized magnetic flux model

questiontext.text: A model for quantized motion of an electron in a uniform magnetic field \(B\) states that the flux passing through the orbit of the electron is \(n(h/e)\) where \(n\) is an integer, \(h\) is Planck's constant and \(e\) is the magnitude of electron's charge. According to the model, the magnetic moment of an electron in its lowest energy state will be (\(m\) is the mass of the electron)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Magnetic flux through electron orbit: \(\Phi = n \left(\frac{h}{e}\right)\)
- Mass of electron = \(m\), charge magnitude = \(e\)
- Magnetic field = \(B\)
- For lowest energy state, \(n = 1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Electron moves in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) perpendicular to uniform magnetic field \(B\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Magnetic flux condition for \(n = 1\): \[ B \pi r^2 = \frac{h}{e} \implies \pi r^2 = \frac{h}{e B} \] - Centripetal acceleration supplied by magnetic force: \[ \frac{m v^2}{r} = e v B \implies v = \frac{e B r}{m} \] - Equivalent current of orbiting electron: \[ I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{e v}{2\pi r} = \frac{e^2 B}{2\pi m} \] - Magnetic moment of orbiting electron: \[ \mu = I \cdot A = I (\pi r^2) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(I\) and \(\pi r^2\) into the magnetic moment equation: \[ \mu = \left( \frac{e^2 B}{2\pi m} \right) \left( \frac{h}{e B} \right) \] \[ \mu = \frac{e h}{2\pi m} = \frac{he}{2\pi m} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Magnetic moment expression \(\frac{he}{2\pi m}\) matches the units of \(\text{A m}^2\) or \(\text{J T}^{-1}\).
- Final Answer: \(\frac{he}{2\pi m}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q19 - Ratio of junction temperatures for three heat conducting rods

questiontext.text: Three identical heat conducting rods are connected in series as shown in the figure. The rods on the sides have thermal conductivity \(2K\) while that in the middle has thermal conductivity \(K\). The left end of the combination is maintained at temperature \(3T\) and the right end at \(T\). The rods are thermally insulated from outside. In steady state, temperature at the left junction is \(T_1\) and that at the right junction is \(T_2\). The ratio \(T_1/T_2\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Three identical length \(L\) and cross-sectional area \(A\) rods in series.
- Thermal conductivities: Left rod = \(2K\), Middle rod = \(K\), Right rod = \(2K\)
- Boundary temperatures: Leftmost end = \(3T\), Rightmost end = \(T\)
- Junction temperatures: Left junction = \(T_1\), Right junction = \(T_2\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Steady-state heat flow (constant heat current \(H\) through all rods).
- Thermal resistance formula: \(R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{k A}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Thermal resistance of side rods: \(R_1 = R_3 = \frac{L}{2KA} = R_0\)
- Thermal resistance of middle rod: \(R_2 = \frac{L}{KA} = 2 R_0\)
- Heat current in steady state: \[ H = \frac{\Delta T_{\text{total}}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{3T - T}{R_0 + 2 R_0 + R_0} = \frac{2T}{4 R_0} = \frac{T}{2 R_0} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate junction temperature \(T_1\) from left rod heat current: \[ 3T - T_1 = H \cdot R_0 = \frac{T}{2 R_0} \cdot R_0 = \frac{T}{2} \implies T_1 = 3T - \frac{T}{2} = \frac{5T}{2} \] - Calculate junction temperature \(T_2\) from right rod heat current: \[ T_2 - T = H \cdot R_0 = \frac{T}{2 R_0} \cdot R_0 = \frac{T}{2} \implies T_2 = T + \frac{T}{2} = \frac{3T}{2} \] - Compute ratio \(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\): \[ \frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{5T / 2}{3T / 2} = \frac{5}{3} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The ratio \(\frac{5}{3}\) matches the temperature drops across the symmetric series combination.
- Final Answer: \(\frac{5}{3}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q20 - Dielectric constant of slab in parallel plate capacitor

questiontext.text:
The plates of a parallel plate capacitor are separated by \(d\). Two slabs of different dielectric constant \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) with thickness \(\frac{3}{8}d\) and \(\frac{d}{2}\), respectively are inserted in the capacitor. Due to this, the capacitance becomes two times larger than when there is nothing between the plates.

If \(K_1 = 1.25 K_2\), the value of \(K_1\) is :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Plate separation = \(d\)
- Initial capacitance without dielectric, \(C_0 = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}\)
- Thickness of dielectric 1, \(t_1 = \frac{3}{8}d\)
- Thickness of dielectric 2, \(t_2 = \frac{d}{2} = \frac{4}{8}d\)
- Remaining air gap thickness, \(t_{\text{air}} = d - \frac{3}{8}d - \frac{4}{8}d = \frac{1}{8}d\)
- New capacitance, \(C = 2 C_0\)
- Relation between dielectric constants: \(K_1 = 1.25 K_2 = \frac{5}{4} K_2 \implies K_2 = 0.8 K_1\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- The dielectric slabs are placed parallel to the capacitor plates.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Capacitance of a multi-layered capacitor: \[ C = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{t_{\text{air}} + \frac{t_1}{K_1} + \frac{t_2}{K_2}} \] - Equating \(C = 2 C_0 = \frac{2 \epsilon_0 A}{d}\): \[ t_{\text{air}} + \frac{t_1}{K_1} + \frac{t_2}{K_2} = \frac{d}{2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute thicknesses into the equation: \[ \frac{d}{8} + \frac{3d}{8 K_1} + \frac{4d}{8 K_2} = \frac{d}{2} \] - Divide both sides by \(\frac{d}{8}\): \[ 1 + \frac{3}{K_1} + \frac{4}{K_2} = 4 \implies \frac{3}{K_1} + \frac{4}{K_2} = 3 \] - Substitute \(K_2 = 0.8 K_1\): \[ \frac{3}{K_1} + \frac{4}{0.8 K_1} = 3 \] \[ \frac{3}{K_1} + \frac{5}{K_1} = 3 \implies \frac{8}{K_1} = 3 \] \[ K_1 = \frac{8}{3} \approx 2.66 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Value \(K_1 = 2.66\) is greater than 1, satisfying physical properties of dielectric materials.
- Final Answer: \(2.66\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q21 - Period of bus service and speed of buses

questiontext.text: Two cities X and Y are connected by a regular bus service with a bus leaving in either direction every T min. A girl is driving scooty with a speed of \(60\text{ km/h}\) in the direction X to Y notices that a bus goes past her every \(30\text{ minutes}\) in the direction of her motion, and every \(10\text{ minutes}\) in the opposite direction. Choose the correct option for the period T of the bus service and the speed (assumed constant) of the buses.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Speed of scooty, \(v = 60\text{ km/h}\)
- Time interval between buses in direction of motion, \(t_1 = 30\text{ min}\)
- Time interval between buses in opposite direction, \(t_2 = 10\text{ min}\)
- Constant speed of buses = \(V\)
- Bus service time interval = \(T\text{ min}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Distance between consecutive buses leaving from either station is \(d = V \times T\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Relative speed in same direction: \(V_{\text{rel1}} = V - 60\)
- Relative speed in opposite direction: \(V_{\text{rel2}} = V + 60\)
- Time interval relations: \[ (V - 60) \times 30 = V \times T \] \[ (V + 60) \times 10 = V \times T \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Equating distance expressions: \[ 30(V - 60) = 10(V + 60) \] \[ 3(V - 60) = V + 60 \] \[ 3V - 180 = V + 60 \implies 2V = 240 \implies V = 120\text{ km/h} \] - Substitute \(V = 120\text{ km/h}\) into second relation: \[ (120 + 60) \times 10 = 120 \times T \] \[ 180 \times 10 = 120 \times T \implies T = \frac{1800}{120} = 15\text{ min} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Checking time interval: Buses pass every 15 min when stationary. With scooty moving at 60 km/h and buses at 120 km/h, relative times match 30 min and 10 min.

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q22 - Friction force exerted by floor on leaning uniform rod

questiontext.text: A uniform rod of mass \(20\text{ kg}\) and length \(5\text{ m}\) leans against a smooth vertical wall making an angle of \(60^\circ\) with it. The other end rests on a rough horizontal floor. The friction force that the floor exerts on the rod is (take \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Mass of uniform rod, \(m = 20\text{ kg}\)
- Length of rod, \(L = 5\text{ m}\)
- Angle with smooth vertical wall = \(60^\circ \implies\) Angle with horizontal floor, \(\theta = 30^\circ\)
- Acceleration due to gravity, \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
- Weight of rod, \(W = m g = 20 \times 10 = 200\text{ N}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- System is in rotational and translational equilibrium.
- Vertical wall is smooth, so normal reaction \(N_W\) from the wall is purely horizontal.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Vertical force balance: \(N_F = W = 200\text{ N}\)
- Horizontal force balance: \(f_{\text{s}} = N_W\)
- Rotational equilibrium condition about base on floor: \[ \sum \tau_{\text{base}} = 0 \implies N_W (L \sin 30^\circ) - W \left(\frac{L}{2} \cos 30^\circ\right) = 0 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Solve for normal force from wall \(N_W\): \[ N_W \sin 30^\circ = \frac{W}{2} \cos 30^\circ \] \[ N_W = \frac{W}{2} \cot 30^\circ = \frac{200\text{ N}}{2} \times \sqrt{3} = 100\sqrt{3}\text{ N} \] - From horizontal equilibrium, friction force \(f_{\text{s}} = N_W\): \[ f_{\text{s}} = 100\sqrt{3}\text{ N} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The static friction force counterbalances the wall's normal force of \(100\sqrt{3}\text{ N}\).
- Final Answer: \(100\sqrt{3}\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q23 - Time dependence of frequency and amplitude for leaky sand box

questiontext.text: In an oscillating spring mass system, a spring is connected to a box filled with sand. As the box oscillates, sand leaks slowly out of the box vertically so that the average frequency \(\omega(t)\) and average amplitude \(A(t)\) of the system change with time \(t\). Which one of the following options schematically depicts these changes correctly?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
- Determine how decreasing mass affects angular frequency \(\omega\) and oscillation amplitude \(A\) in simple harmonic motion.

Step 2: Angular Frequency Evaluation
- Angular frequency of spring-mass system: \[ \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \] - As sand leaks out vertically, total mass \(m(t)\) decreases with time.
- Since \(\omega \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\), angular frequency \(\omega(t)\) increases with time \(t\).

Step 3: Amplitude Evaluation
- Under gravity, spring equilibrium compression/extension is \(x_0 = \frac{m g}{k}\). As mass leaks out, the equilibrium position shifts upward.
- Additionally, leaking sand carries away kinetic energy vertically, causing mechanical energy and effective amplitude \(A(t)\) to decrease with time \(t\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
- Angular frequency \(\omega(t)\) increases monotonically over time while amplitude \(A(t)\) decreases monotonically over time.
- Final Answer: Schematic graph showing increasing \(\omega(t)\) and decreasing \(A(t)\) over time.

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q24 - Exponents for deflation time of gas filled balloon

questiontext.text: A balloon is made of a material of surface tension \(S\) and its inflation outlet (from where gas is filled in it) has small area \(A\). It is filled with a gas of density \(\rho\) and takes a spherical shape of radius \(R\). When the gas is allowed to flow freely out of it, its radius \(r\) changes from \(R\) to \(0\) (zero) in time \(T\). If the speed \(v(r)\) of gas coming out of the balloon depends on \(r\) as \(r^a\) and \(T \propto S^\alpha A^\beta \rho^\gamma R^\delta\) then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Surface tension of balloon material = \(S\)
- Outlet area = \(A\)
- Gas density = \(\rho\)
- Initial radius = \(R\), final radius = \(0\)
- Gas outflow speed \(v(r) \propto r^a\)
- Deflation time \(T \propto S^\alpha A^\beta \rho^\gamma R^\delta\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Gas flow is non-viscous and obeys Bernoulli's principle.
- Excess pressure inside spherical balloon: \(\Delta P \propto \frac{S}{r}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- From Bernoulli's equation for gas exit velocity: \[ \Delta P = \frac{1}{2} \rho v(r)^2 \implies v(r) = \sqrt{\frac{2 \Delta P}{\rho}} \propto \sqrt{\frac{S}{\rho r}} = S^{1/2} \rho^{-1/2} r^{-1/2} \] Thus, \(a = -\frac{1}{2}\).
- Rate of volume decrease of balloon: \[ -\frac{dV}{dt} = A \cdot v(r) \implies -4\pi r^2 \frac{dr}{dt} \propto A S^{1/2} \rho^{-1/2} r^{-1/2} \] \[ -r^{5/2} dr \propto A S^{1/2} \rho^{-1/2} dt \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Integrate from \(r = R\) to \(0\): \[ \int_0^R r^{5/2} dr \propto A S^{1/2} \rho^{-1/2} T \] \[ \frac{R^{7/2}}{7/2} \propto A S^{1/2} \rho^{-1/2} T \] - Solve for time \(T\): \[ T \propto S^{-1/2} A^{-1} \rho^{1/2} R^{7/2} \] - Matching powers: \[ \alpha = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad \beta = -1, \quad \gamma = \frac{1}{2}, \quad \delta = \frac{7}{2}, \quad a = -\frac{1}{2} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Exponents match dimensional and hydrodynamic equations.
- Final Answer: \(a = -\frac{1}{2}, \alpha = -\frac{1}{2}, \beta = -1, \gamma = \frac{1}{2}, \delta = \frac{7}{2}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q25 - Diameter measurement using Vernier callipers with zero error

questiontext.text:
Consider the diameter of a spherical object being measured with the help of a Vernier callipers. Suppose its \(10\text{ Vernier Scale Divisions (V.S.D.)}\) are equal to its \(9\text{ Main Scale Divisions (M.S.D.)}\). The least division in the M.S. is \(0.1\text{ cm}\) and the zero of V.S. is at \(x = 0.1\text{ cm}\) when the jaws of Vernier callipers are closed.

If the main scale reading for the diameter is \(M = 5\text{ cm}\) and the number of coinciding vernier division is \(8\), the measured diameter after zero error correction, is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- \(10\text{ VSD} = 9\text{ MSD}\)
- Main scale division value, \(1\text{ MSD} = 0.1\text{ cm}\)
- Position of Vernier zero when jaws closed, \(x = +0.1\text{ cm} \implies \text{Zero Error (Z.E.)} = +0.1\text{ cm}\)
- Main scale reading, \(M = 5\text{ cm}\)
- Vernier coinciding division, \(n = 8\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Least Count (L.C.) formula for Vernier Callipers applies.
- Corrected Reading = Observed Reading - Zero Error.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Least Count calculation: \[ 1\text{ VSD} = 0.9\text{ MSD} \] \[ \text{L.C.} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = 0.1\text{ MSD} = 0.1 \times 0.1\text{ cm} = 0.01\text{ cm} \] - Observed reading: \[ \text{Observed Reading} = M + (n \times \text{L.C.}) \] - True reading: \[ \text{Corrected Reading} = \text{Observed Reading} - \text{Zero Error} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate Observed Reading: \[ \text{Observed Reading} = 5\text{ cm} + (8 \times 0.01\text{ cm}) = 5.08\text{ cm} \] - Apply zero error correction: \[ \text{Corrected Reading} = 5.08\text{ cm} - (+0.1\text{ cm}) = 4.98\text{ cm} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Positive zero error of \(0.1\text{ cm}\) must be subtracted from observed reading \(5.08\text{ cm}\) to yield \(4.98\text{ cm}\).
- Final Answer: \(4.98\text{ cm}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q26 - Magnetic field due to displacement current in charging capacitor

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor made of circular plates is being charged such that the surface charge density on its plates is increasing at a constant rate with time. The magnetic field arising due to displacement current is :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
- Analyze the magnetic field induced inside and outside circular capacitor plates due to displacement current during charging.

Step 2: Field Derivation Using Ampere-Maxwell Law
- Surface charge density rate \(\frac{d\sigma}{dt} = \text{constant}\).
- Electric field between capacitor plates: \(E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\).
- Displacement current density: \[ J_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{dE}{dt} = \frac{d\sigma}{dt} = \text{constant} \]
- Inside the plates at radial distance \(r < R\) (where \(R\) is plate radius): \[ \oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{d,\text{enclosed}} \implies B (2\pi r) = \mu_0 (J_d \pi r^2) \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 J_d r}{2} \propto r \]
- Outside the plates at radial distance \(r > R\): \[ B (2\pi r) = \mu_0 (J_d \pi R^2) \implies B = \frac{\mu_0 J_d R^2}{2r} \propto \frac{1}{r} \]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
- The magnetic field is non-zero everywhere, increases linearly from zero at the center to a maximum at the periphery \(r = R\), and decreases as \(\frac{1}{r}\) outside.
- Final Answer: non-zero everywhere with maximum at the imaginary cylindrical surface connecting peripheries of the plates

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q28 - Repulsive force between conducting spheres after charge sharing

questiontext.text: Two identical charged conducting spheres A and B have their centres separated by a certain distance. Charge on each sphere is \(q\) and the force of repulsion between them is \(F\). A third identical uncharged conducting sphere is brought in contact with sphere A first and then with B and finally removed from both. New force of repulsion between spheres A and B (Radii of A and B are negligible compared to the distance of separation so that for calculating force between them they can be considered as point charges) is best given as :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Initial charge on sphere A = \(q\)
- Initial charge on sphere B = \(q\)
- Separation distance = \(d\)
- Initial repulsive force, \(F = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q^2}{d^2}\)
- Sphere C is identical and uncharged (initial charge = 0).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Equal redistribution of charge occurs when identical conducting spheres are brought into contact.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Coulomb's Law: \[ F = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{d^2} \] - Charge sharing between two identical conducting spheres: \[ q_{\text{final}} = \frac{q_1 + q_2}{2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- When sphere C (charge 0) touches sphere A (charge \(q\)): \[ q_A' = q_C' = \frac{q + 0}{2} = \frac{q}{2} \] - When sphere C (now charge \(\frac{q}{2}\)) touches sphere B (charge \(q\)): \[ q_B' = \frac{\frac{q}{2} + q}{2} = \frac{3q}{4} \] - New repulsive force between A and B: \[ F' = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q_A' q_B'}{d^2} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{\left(\frac{q}{2}\right) \left(\frac{3q}{4}\right)}{d^2} \] \[ F' = \frac{3}{8} \left( \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q^2}{d^2} \right) = \frac{3F}{8} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The new electrostatic force is \(\frac{3}{8}\) times the original force \(F\).
- Final Answer: \(\frac{3F}{8}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q29 - Equilibrium pressure of ideal gas mixture in two chambers

The chambers contains \(n_1 = 5\) and \(n_2 = 4\text{ moles}\) of ideal gas at pressures \(p_1 = 1\text{ atm}\) and \(p_2 = 2\text{ atm}\), respectively. name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q30 - Orbit radius and speed dependence in constant force Bohr model

questiontext.text: A particle of mass \(m\) is moving around the origin with a constant force \(F\) pulling it towards the origin. If Bohr model is used to describe its motion, the radius \(r\) of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit and the particle's speed \(v\) in the orbit depend on \(n\) as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Constant magnitude central force = \(F\)
- Mass of particle = \(m\)
- Bohr angular momentum quantization: \(m v r = \frac{n h}{2\pi} \implies v \propto \frac{n}{r}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Circular orbital motion about origin under constant inward attractive force \(F\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Centripetal force balance: \[ \frac{m v^2}{r} = F \implies v = \sqrt{\frac{F r}{m}} \implies v \propto r^{1/2} \] - Combining with Bohr quantization relation \(v \propto \frac{n}{r}\): \[ r^{1/2} \propto \frac{n}{r} \implies r^{3/2} \propto n \implies r \propto n^{2/3} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(r \propto n^{2/3}\) into speed relation \(v \propto r^{1/2}\): \[ v \propto (n^{2/3})^{1/2} \implies v \propto n^{1/3} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Product \(m v r \propto n^{1/3} \cdot n^{2/3} = n^1\), confirming angular momentum quantization.
- Final Answer: \(r \propto n^{2/3};\quad v \propto n^{1/3}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q31 - Orbital period of Mercury using Kepler third law

questiontext.text: The radius of Martian orbit around the Sun is about 4 times the radius of the orbit of Mercury. The Martian year is 687 Earth days. Then which of the following is the length of 1 year on Mercury ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions

- Period of Mars, \(T_{\text{Mars}} = 687\text{ Earth days}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Planetary orbits are approximated as circular orbits around the Sun.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Kepler's Third Law of Planetary Motion: \[ T^2 \propto R^3 \implies \left(\frac{T_{\text{Mercury}}}{T_{\text{Mars}}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{R_{\text{Mercury}}}{R_{\text{Mars}}}\right)^3 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(R_{\text{Mars}} = 4 R_{\text{Mercury}}\): \[ \left(\frac{T_{\text{Mercury}}}{687}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{64} \] - Take square root of both sides: \[ \frac{T_{\text{Mercury}}}{687} = \frac{1}{8} \] \[ T_{\text{Mercury}} = \frac{687}{8} = 85.875\text{ Earth days} \approx 88\text{ Earth days} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Mercury is closer to the Sun and takes approximately 88 Earth days per orbit.
- Final Answer: \(88\text{ earth days}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q32 - Gravitational force at height one-third Earth radius

questiontext.text: A body weighs \(48\text{ N}\) on the surface of the earth. The gravitational force experienced by the body due to the earth at a height equal to one-third the radius of the earth from its surface is :

- Height above surface, \(h = \frac{R}{3}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Acceleration due to gravity varies inversely with the square of distance from the Earth's center.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Gravitational force at height \(h\): \[ F = W_0 \left( \frac{R}{R + h} \right)^2 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q36 - Current through central branch of resistor bridge

questiontext.text: A constant voltage of \(50\text{ V}\) is maintained between the points A and B of the circuit shown in the figure. The current through the branch CD of the circuit is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions

- Resistor network: \(1\ \Omega\) (top-left), \(2\ \Omega\) (top-right), \(3\ \Omega\) (bottom-left), \(4\ \Omega\) (bottom-right)
- Branch CD connects junction C (between top resistors) and junction D (between bottom resistors).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Branch CD is a ideal short-circuit wire connecting C and D.
- Set potential at point B as \(V_B = 0\text{ V}\) and point A as \(V_A = 50\text{ V}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL): \(\sum I_{\text{into node}} = \sum I_{\text{out of node}}\)
- Ohm's Law: \(I = \frac{\Delta V}{R}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Apply KCL to node combination C-D: \[ \frac{50 - V_0}{1} + \frac{50 - V_0}{3} = \frac{V_0 - 0}{2} + \frac{V_0 - 0}{4} \] \[ (50 - V_0)\left(1 + \frac{1}{3}\right) = V_0\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) \] \[ (50 - V_0) \times \frac{4}{3} = V_0 \times \frac{3}{4} \] \[ 50 \times \frac{4}{3} = V_0 \left( \frac{3}{4} + \frac{4}{3} \right) = V_0 \times \frac{25}{12} \] \[ V_0 = \frac{200 / 3}{25 / 12} = 32\text{ V} \] - Calculate current into node C from top-left resistor: \[ I_{AC} = \frac{50 - 32}{1\ \Omega} = 18\text{ A} \] - Calculate current out of node C to top-right resistor: \[ I_{CB} = \frac{32 - 0}{2\ \Omega} = 16\text{ A} \] - Apply KCL at node C to find current in branch CD: \[ I_{CD} = I_{AC} - I_{CB} = 18\text{ A} - 16\text{ A} = 2.0\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Verify at node D: Current into D from bottom-left resistor is \(\frac{50 - 32}{3} = 6\text{ A}\). Current from C is \(2\text{ A}\). Total current leaving D = \(6 + 2 = 8\text{ A}\), which matches \(\frac{32}{4} = 8\text{ A}\).

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q41 - Ratio of piston radii for gas expansion under constant pressure

questiontext.text: Two gases \(A\) and \(B\) are filled at the same pressure in separate cylinders with movable pistons of radius \(r_A\) and \(r_B\), respectively. On supplying an equal amount of heat to both the systems reversibly under constant pressure, the pistons of gas \(A\) and \(B\) are displaced by \(16\text{ cm}\) and \(9\text{ cm}\), respectively. If the change in their internal energy is the same, then the ratio \(r_A/r_B\) is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Pressures are equal: \(P_A = P_B = P\)
- Heat supplied is equal: \(Q_A = Q_B = Q\)
- Internal energy change is equal: \(\Delta U_A = \Delta U_B = \Delta U\)
- Displacement of piston A, \(\Delta x_A = 16\text{ cm}\)
- Displacement of piston B, \(\Delta x_B = 9\text{ cm}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Both gas expansions occur reversibly at constant pressure.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- First Law of Thermodynamics: \[ Q = \Delta U + W \implies W = Q - \Delta U \] Since \(Q\) and \(\Delta U\) are identical for both systems, work done is equal: \(W_A = W_B\).
- Isobaric work done: \[ W = P \Delta V = P (A \cdot \Delta x) = P (\pi r^2 \Delta x) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Equating work done for gases A and B: \[ P \pi r_A^2 \Delta x_A = P \pi r_B^2 \Delta x_B \implies r_A^2 \Delta x_A = r_B^2 \Delta x_B \] - Substitute displacement values: \[ r_A^2 \times 16 = r_B^2 \times 9 \implies \frac{r_A^2}{r_B^2} = \frac{9}{16} \] - Take square root: \[ \frac{r_A}{r_B} = \frac{3}{4} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The ratio of piston radii \(\frac{r_A}{r_B}\) is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
- Final Answer: \(\frac{3}{4}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Maximum relative error combination rule applies for small fractional errors.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Maximum relative percentage error in \(P\): \[ \frac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 = 3\left(\frac{\Delta a}{a} \times 100\right) + 2\left(\frac{\Delta b}{b} \times 100\right) + 1\left(\frac{\Delta c}{c} \times 100\right) + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\Delta d}{d} \times 100\right) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute given error percentages: \[ \frac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 = 3(1\%) + 2(3\%) + 1(2\%) + \frac{1}{2}(4\%) \] \[ \frac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 = 3\% + 6\% + 2\% + 2\% = 13\% \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q43 - Transmitted light intensity through three polaroids

questiontext.text: The intensity of transmitted light when a polaroid sheet, placed between two crossed polaroids at \(22.5^\circ\) from the polarization axis of one of the polaroid, is (\(I_0\) is the intensity of polarised light after passing through the first polaroid):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Intensity after first polaroid = \(I_0\)
- Angle between first polaroid and second (middle) polaroid, \(\theta = 22.5^\circ\)
- First and third polaroids are crossed (\(90^\circ\) relative angle), so angle between second and third polaroid is \(\theta' = 90^\circ - 22.5^\circ = 67.5^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Malus's Law applies to ideal polaroid sheets.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Malus's Law: \(I = I_{\text{in}} \cos^2 \theta\)
- Intensity after middle polaroid: \[ I_1 = I_0 \cos^2 (22.5^\circ) \]
- Intensity after third polaroid: \[ I_2 = I_1 \cos^2 (67.5^\circ) = I_0 \cos^2 (22.5^\circ) \sin^2 (22.5^\circ) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Using double angle trigonometric identity \(\sin(2\theta) = 2 \sin\theta \cos\theta\): \[ \sin(22.5^\circ) \cos(22.5^\circ) = \frac{\sin(45^\circ)}{2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \] - Squaring both sides: \[ I_2 = I_0 \left( \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \right)^2 = \frac{I_0}{8} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Transmitted intensity after passing three polaroids is \(\frac{I_0}{8}\).
- Final Answer: \(\frac{I_0}{8}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q44 - Ratio of oscillation amplitudes for equal maximum speeds

questiontext.text: Two identical point masses P and Q, suspended from two separate massless springs of spring constants \(k_1\) and \(k_2\), respectively, oscillate vertically. If their maximum speeds are the same, the ratio \((A_Q/A_P)\) of the amplitude \(A_Q\) of mass \(Q\) to the amplitude \(A_P\) of mass \(P\) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Identical masses: \(m_P = m_Q = m\)
- Spring constants: \(k_1\) for P and \(k_2\) for Q
- Maximum speed condition: \(v_{\text{max}, P} = v_{\text{max}, Q}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Undamped vertical simple harmonic motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Angular frequency of spring-mass oscillator: \[ \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \] - Maximum speed formula in SHM: \[ v_{\text{max}} = \omega A \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Express maximum speeds: \[ v_{\text{max}, P} = \sqrt{\frac{k_1}{m}} A_P \] \[ v_{\text{max}, Q} = \sqrt{\frac{k_2}{m}} A_Q \] - Equating the maximum speeds: \[ \sqrt{\frac{k_1}{m}} A_P = \sqrt{\frac{k_2}{m}} A_Q \] - Rearranging to isolate \(\frac{A_Q}{A_P}\): \[ \frac{A_Q}{A_P} = \frac{\sqrt{k_1}}{\sqrt{k_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{k_1}{k_2}} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The ratio of amplitudes \(\frac{A_Q}{A_P}\) is \(\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{k_2}}\).
- Final Answer: \(\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{k_2}}\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q45 - Fundamental frequency of open pipe half submerged in water

questiontext.text: A pipe open at both ends has a fundamental frequency \(f\) in air. The pipe is now dipped vertically in a water drum to half of its length. The fundamental frequency of the air column is now equal to :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Length of pipe = \(L\)
- Initial fundamental frequency (open at both ends) = \(f\)
- Pipe dipped to half length in water: new air column length \(L' = \frac{L}{2}\) with one end closed by water.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Speed of sound in air is constant = \(v\).
- End corrections are neglected.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Fundamental frequency of pipe open at both ends: \[ f = \frac{v}{2L} \] - Fundamental frequency of pipe closed at one end of length \(L'\): \[ f' = \frac{v}{4 L'} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Substitute \(L' = \frac{L}{2}\) into closed pipe formula: \[ f' = \frac{v}{4 \left(\frac{L}{2}\right)} = \frac{v}{2L} = f \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- The new fundamental frequency is equal to the original frequency \(f\).
- Final Answer: \(f\)

name.text: NEET_PHYSICS_2025_MCQ_Q46 - Ratio of wavelengths absorbed in hydrogen atom transitions

questiontext.text: The ratio of the wavelengths of the light absorbed by a Hydrogen atom when it undergoes \(n = 2 \rightarrow n = 3\) and \(n = 4 \rightarrow n = 6\) transitions, respectively, is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Transition 1: \(n = 2 \rightarrow n = 3\)
- Transition 2: \(n = 4 \rightarrow n = 6\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
- Rydberg formula for hydrogen (\(Z = 1\)) applies.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Rydberg formula for absorbed wavelength: \[ \frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Calculate \(\lambda_1\) for \(n = 2 \rightarrow 3\): \[ \frac{1}{\lambda_1} = R \left( \frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9} \right) = \frac{5R}{36} \implies \lambda_1 = \frac{36}{5R} \] - Calculate \(\lambda_2\) for \(n = 4 \rightarrow 6\): \[ \frac{1}{\lambda_2} = R \left( \frac{1}{4^2} - \frac{1}{6^2} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{16} - \frac{1}{36} \right) = R \left( \frac{9 - 4}{144} \right) = \frac{5R}{144} \implies \lambda_2 = \frac{144}{5R} \] - Ratio \(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\): \[ \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \frac{36 / (5R)}{144 / (5R)} = \frac{36}{144} = \frac{1}{4} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
- Ratio simplifies to \(\frac{1}{4}\).
- Final Answer: \(\frac{1}{4}\)

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_MCQ_Q47 - True statements on periodic properties of elements

questiontext.text:

C. Ar, \(\text{K}^{+}\), \(\text{Cl}^{-}\), \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\), and \(\text{S}^{2-}\) are all isoelectronic species.
D. The correct order of the first ionization enthalpies of Na, Mg, Al, and Si is \(\text{Si} > \text{Al} > \text{Mg} > \text{Na}\).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
- Statement A is incorrect because gallium (Ga) has a unusually low melting point (\(303\text{ K}\)).
- Statement B is incorrect because on the Pauling scale, both nitrogen (N) and chlorine (Cl) have the same electronegativity value of \(3.0\).
- Statement C is correct because \(\text{Ar}\), \(\text{K}^+\), \(\text{Cl}^-\), \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\), and \(\text{S}^{2-}\) all contain 18 electrons, making them isoelectronic.

- Statement E is correct because atomic radius increases down Group 1 (\(\text{Li} < \text{Rb} < \text{Cs}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
- Statements C and E only are true.
- Final Answer: C and E only

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_MCQ_Q50 - Energy and radius of first Bohr orbit for He+ and Li2+

questiontext.text:
Energy and radius of first Bohr orbit of \(\text{He}^+\) and \(\text{Li}^{2+}\) are

[Given \(R_H = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}\), \(a_0 = 52.9\text{ pm}\)]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Formulae
- Ground state Rydberg energy constant, \(R_H = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}\)
- Ground state Bohr radius, \(a_0 = 52.9\text{ pm}\)
- Bohr energy formula: \(E_n = -R_H \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\)
- Bohr radius formula: \(r_n = a_0 \frac{n^2}{Z}\)

Step 2: Calculation for \(\text{Li}^{2+}\) (\(Z = 3, n = 1\))
- Energy: \[ E_1(\text{Li}^{2+}) = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J} \times \frac{3^2}{1^2} = -19.62 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J} \] - Radius: \[ r_1(\text{Li}^{2+}) = 52.9\text{ pm} \times \frac{1^2}{3} \approx 17.6\text{ pm} \]

Step 3: Calculation for \(\text{He}^+\) (\(Z = 2, n = 1\))
- Energy: \[ E_1(\text{He}^+) = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J} \times \frac{2^2}{1^2} = -8.72 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J} \] - Radius: \[ r_1(\text{He}^+) = 52.9\text{ pm} \times \frac{1^2}{2} \approx 26.4\text{ pm} \]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
- The energy and radius values are \(E_n(\text{Li}^{2+}) = -19.62 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}\), \(r_n(\text{Li}^{2+}) = 17.6\text{ pm}\) and \(E_n(\text{He}^+) = -8.72 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}\), \(r_n(\text{He}^+) = 26.4\text{ pm}\).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_MCQ_Q56 - Time required for 99.9 percentage completion of first order reaction

questiontext.text: If the half-life (\(t_{1/2}\)) for a first order reaction is \(1\text{ minute}\), then the time required for \(99.9\%\) completion of the reaction is closest to :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Half-life, \(t_{1/2} = 1\text{ min}\)
- Percentage completion = \(99.9\%\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- First-order rate constant: \[ k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{1\text{ min}} \]
- First-order kinetic equation: \[ t = \frac{2.303}{k} \log \left( \frac{[A]_0}{[A]} \right) \]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(99.9\%\) completion, remaining concentration \([A] = [A]_0 - 0.999 [A]_0 = 0.001 [A]_0 = 10^{-3} [A]_0\): \[ t_{99.9\%} = \frac{2.303}{0.693} \log \left( \frac{[A]_0}{10^{-3} [A]_0} \right) \] \[ t_{99.9\%} = \frac{2.303}{0.693} \log(10^3) = \frac{2.303 \times 3}{0.693} \approx 9.97\text{ minutes} \approx 10\text{ minutes} \]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
- \(t_{99.9\%} \approx 10 \times t_{1/2} = 10 \times 1 = 10\text{ minutes}\).
- Final Answer: 10 minutes

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_MCQ_Q57 - Order of absorbed light wavelength for transition metal complexes

questiontext.text:
The correct order of the wavelength of light absorbed by the following complexes is,

Step 2: Evaluation of Crystal Field Splitting (\(\Delta_o\))

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_MCQ_Q59 - Ionization constant relations for polyprotic phosphoric acid

questiontext.text:
Phosphoric acid ionizes in three steps with their ionization constant values \(K_{a_1}\), \(K_{a_2}\) and \(K_{a_3}\), respectively, while \(K\) is the overall ionization constant. Which of the following statements are true?

A. \(\log K = \log K_{a_1} + \log K_{a_2} + \log K_{a_3}\)
B. \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) is a stronger acid than \(\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-\) and \(\text{HPO}_4^{2-}\).
C. \(K_{a_1} > K_{a_2} > K_{a_3}\)
D. \(K_{a_1} = \frac{K_{a_3} + K_{a_2}}{2}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
- Analyze step-wise ionization of polyprotic acids in aqueous solution.

Step 2: Statement Analysis
- For step-wise ionization, overall equilibrium constant \(K = K_{a_1} \times K_{a_2} \times K_{a_3}\). Taking logarithm yields \(\log K = \log K_{a_1} + \log K_{a_2} + \log K_{a_3}\) (Statement A is true).
- Neutral \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) loses a proton much more readily than negatively charged ions \(\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-\) and \(\text{HPO}_4^{2-}\), making \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) the strongest acid among them (Statement B is true).
- Removing successive protons against increasing negative charge becomes increasingly difficult, so \(K_{a_1} > K_{a_2} > K_{a_3}\) (Statement C is true).
- Statement D is false because ionization constants decrease by orders of magnitude rather than linearly.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
- Statements A, B and C only are true.
- Final Answer: A, B and C only

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_MCQ_Q60 - Reaction not producing benzene as product

As bond order increases, the attractive force between the nuclei increases, drawing the atoms closer together and decreasing the bond length. Thus, bond order is inversely proportional to bond length. Therefore, Statement II is false.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

\(K_p\) for the reaction at \(1000\mathrm{~K}\) is

generalfeedback.text:

Backward rate constant \(k_b = 2500 \cdot k_f\)
Temperature \(T = 1000\mathrm{~K}\)

Reaction: \(\mathrm{A}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{B}(g)\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Ideal gas behavior is assumed for reactants and products under given conditions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Equilibrium constant in terms of concentration: \(K_c = \frac{k_f}{k_b}\)

The equilibrium constant \(K_p\) for the reaction at \(1000\mathrm{~K}\) is \(0.033\).

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_Q81 - Deviation from Raoult's law for binary liquid mixture

Moles of liquid X: \(n_X = 5\mathrm{~mol}\)

Observed total vapour pressure: \(P_{\text{obs}} = 70\mathrm{~torr}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Ideal solution behavior follows Raoult's law.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Mole fraction of X: \(x_X = \frac{n_X}{n_X + n_Y}\)
Mole fraction of Y: \(x_Y = \frac{n_Y}{n_X + n_Y}\)
Ideal total vapour pressure: \(P_{\text{ideal}} = P_X^\circ x_X + P_Y^\circ x_Y\)

\[x_X = \frac{5}{5 + 10} = \frac{1}{3}, \quad x_Y = \frac{10}{5 + 10} = \frac{2}{3}\]

Since \(P_{\text{obs}} = 70\mathrm{~torr} < P_{\text{ideal}} = 73\mathrm{~torr}\), the attractive forces between unlike molecules are stronger than those between like molecules.

Because the observed vapour pressure is lower than predicted by Raoult's law, the solution exhibits negative deviation.

name.text: NEET_CHEMISTRY_2025_Q89 - Time required for first order reactant reduction

questiontext.text:
If the rate constant of a reaction is 0.03 s-1, how much time does it take for 7.2 mol L-1 concentration of the reactant to get reduced to 0.9 mol L-1?

(Given: log 2 = 0.301)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Rate constant \(k = 0.03\mathrm{~s^{-1}}\) (first-order kinetics)
Initial concentration \([A]_0 = 7.2\mathrm{~mol~L^{-1}}\)
Final concentration \([A] = 0.9\mathrm{~mol~L^{-1}}\)
\(\log 2 = 0.301\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a first-order reaction:
\[t = \frac{2.303}{k} \log \frac{[A]_0}{[A]}\]
Alternatively, using half-life \(t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the ratio of concentrations:
\[\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = \frac{7.2}{0.9} = 8 = 2^3\]
Calculate the half-life:
\[t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{0.03} = 23.1\mathrm{~s}\]
Number of half-lives required to reduce concentration from \(7.2\) to \(0.9\) (\(7.2 \rightarrow 3.6 \rightarrow 1.8 \rightarrow 0.9\)) = \(3\).
Total time required:
\[t = 3 \times 23.1\mathrm{~s} = 69.3\mathrm{~s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The required time for the concentration reduction is \(69.3\mathrm{~s}\).

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q105 - Use of streptokinase in blood clot removal

questiontext.text: Streptokinase produced by bacterium Streptococcus is used for

Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering, functions medically as a clot buster enzyme.

It is administered intravenously to dissolve fibrin clots inside blood vessels in patients suffering from myocardial infarction or acute thrombosis.

Streptokinase is used for removing clots from blood vessels.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q106 - Human chromosome with highest number of genes

questiontext.text: Which chromosome in the human genome has the highest number of genes?

According to the results of the Human Genome Project (HGP), Chromosome 1 contains the largest number of genes in the human genome, totaling 2968 genes.

Step 2: Comparison
Chromosome Y contains the fewest genes (231 genes).

Conclusion
Chromosome 1 has the highest number of genes.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q107 - Location of copulatory pad in male frog

questiontext.text: Which of the following statement is correct about location of the male frog copulatory pad?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Sexual Dimorphism in Frog
Male frogs are distinguished from female frogs by the presence of vocal sacs and specialized copulatory pads (nuptial pads).

Step 2: Anatomical Location
The copulatory pad is situated specifically on the ventral surface of the first digit of the fore limbs in adult male frogs, helping them hold the female during amplexus.

The copulatory pad is located on the first digit of the fore limb.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q108 - Phytohormone promoting nutrient mobilization to delay leaf senescence

questiontext.text: Which one of the following phytohormones promotes nutrient mobilization which helps in the delay of leaf senescence in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physiological Role of Cytokinins
Cytokinins play an essential role in plant growth, cell division, and lateral shoot growth.

Step 2: Senescence Delay Mechanism
Cytokinins promote active nutrient mobilization into tissues, preventing chlorophyll degradation and delaying leaf senescence (Richmond-Lang effect).

Conclusion
Cytokinin is the plant growth regulator that promotes nutrient mobilization to delay leaf senescence.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q109 - Identification of pseudocoelomate body cavity

questiontext.text: While trying to find out the characteristic of a newly found animal, a researcher did the histology of adult animal and observed a cavity with presence of mesodermal tissue towards the body wall but no mesodermal tissue was observed towards the alimentary canal. What could be the possible coelome of that animal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Coelom Types
- True coelom (eucoelom): Body cavity completely lined on both sides (outer body wall and inner gut wall) by mesoderm.
- Pseudocoelom: Body cavity where mesoderm is present as scattered pouches or attached only towards the body wall, leaving the alimentary canal unlined by mesoderm.
- Acoelomate: Body cavity is completely absent.

Step 2: Diagnosis
Since mesodermal tissue is observed towards the body wall but absent along the alimentary canal, the body cavity matches the definition of a pseudocoelom.

Conclusion
The coelom type of the animal is pseudocoelomate.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q110 - Match human sperm structures with physiological functions

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q111 - Sequence of stages in pteridophyte life cycle

questiontext.text:
Given below are the stages in the life cycle of pteridophytes. Arrange the following stages in the correct sequence.

A. Prothallus stage
B. Meiosis in spore mother cells
C. Fertilisation
D. Formation of archegonia and antheridia in gametophyte.
E. Transfer of antherozoids to the archegonia in presence of water.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of Pteridophyte Life Cycle Stages
1. Meiosis occurs in diploid spore mother cells within sporangia to form haploid spores (Stage B).
2. Spores germinate in cool, damp places to form the haploid gametophyte, called the prothallus (Stage A).
3. The prothallus produces multicellular sex organs: archegonia (female) and antheridia (male) (Stage D).
4. Flagellated antherozoids are released and swim through water to reach the mouth of archegonia (Stage E).
5. Fusion of gametes occurs inside archegonia to achieve fertilisation (Stage C).

Conclusion
The correct chronological order is B, A, D, E, C.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q112 - Regulation mechanisms of cardiac activities

questiontext.text:
Cardiac activities of the heart are regulated by :

A. Nodal tissue
B. A special neural centre in the medulla oblongata
C. Adrenal medullary hormones
D. Adrenal cortical hormones

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Myogenic Control (Nodal Tissue)
Normal activities of the heart are regulated intrinsically (myogenically) by specialized nodal tissue (SA node and AV node), making the heart auto-rhythmic (Factor A).

Step 2: Neural Control
A specialized neural center in the medulla oblongata regulates cardiac function through the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic signals) (Factor B).

Step 3: Hormonal Control
Adrenal medullary hormones (adrenaline and noradrenaline) increase heart rate and cardiac output during stress (Factor C).

Step 4: Adrenal Cortical Hormones
Adrenal cortical hormones regulate electrolyte and carbohydrate metabolism rather than directly controlling cardiac rhythm or output.

Conclusion
Cardiac activities are regulated by factors A, B, and C only.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q113 - Non nitrogen fixing organisms

questiontext.text:
Which of following organisms cannot fix nitrogen?

A. Azotobacter
B. Oscillatoria
C. Anabaena
D. Volvox
E. Nostoc

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nitrogen-Fixing Organisms
Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium, whereas Oscillatoria, Anabaena, and Nostoc are nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria equipped with specialized heterocysts or nitrogenase enzyme complexes.

Step 2: Non-Nitrogen-Fixing Organisms
Volvox is a colonial green alga (Chlorophyceae) that carries out photosynthesis but lacks nitrogenase enzymes and cannot fix atmospheric nitrogen.

Conclusion
Volvox (D only) cannot fix nitrogen.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q114 - Statements on RNA interactions and RNA interference

questiontext.text:

Statement II : RNA interference (RNAi) takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Statement I
During protein translation, transfer RNA (tRNA) interacts directly with messenger RNA (mRNA) through codon-anticodon base pairing. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) in the ribosome also interacts structurally and functionally with mRNA during initiation and polypeptide synthesis. Hence, Statement I is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statement II
RNA interference (RNAi) is a gene-silencing mechanism that operates in all eukaryotic organisms as a cellular defense strategy against viral infection and mobile genetic elements (transposons). Hence, Statement II is correct.

Conclusion
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q115 - Selection of recombinant colonies using insertional inactivation

questiontext.text: In the above represented plasmid an alien piece of DNA is inserted at EcoRI site. Which of the following strategies will be chosen to select the recombinant colonies?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Insertional Inactivation Principle
The \(\mathrm{EcoRI}\) restriction site lies within the \(\beta\)-galactosidase coding sequence. Insertion of an alien piece of DNA at this site disrupts the gene, leading to insertional inactivation.

Step 2: Selection Strategy
Non-recombinant colonies retain a functional \(\beta\)-galactosidase gene and hydrolyze chromogenic substrates (such as X-gal) to form blue-colored colonies.
Recombinant colonies lose \(\beta\)-galactosidase activity and fail to produce color, yielding white colonies on medium containing chromogenic substrate.

Conclusion
White color colonies will be selected to identify recombinants.

In 1983, the American pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly synthesized DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin and inserted them into plasmids of a bacterium.

Step 2: Host Organism Identification
The host bacterium used for recombinant production and expression was Escherichia coli.

Conclusion
A bacterium was used to prepare human insulin.

name.text: NEET_BIOLOGY_2025_Q117 - Enzyme class catalyzing group transfer reactions

questiontext.text:
Name the class of enzyme that usually catalyze the following reaction :

\[\mathrm{S} - \mathrm{G} + \mathrm{S}^{\#} \rightarrow \mathrm{S} + \mathrm{S}^{\#} - \mathrm{G}\]

S → a substrate
